newsitem.title: USA: Emus break free, run wild in southern Missouri.
newsitem.headline: Emus break free, run wild in southern Missouri.

text.p: At least 16 emus remained on the loose on Friday in a heavily wooded area of southern Missouri as local conservation and law enforcement authorities refused to help retrieve them.

The Missouri Department of Conservation and the Howell County Sheriff's Department said they were not helping in the hunt for the flightless birds, which can be up to 5 or 6 feet tall, and said their owner was responsible for retrieving them.

The owner, Hiver Gravely, could not be reached for comment on Friday. But Gravely told a local reporter earlier this week that the birds, which are native to Australia, fled from their enclosure, driven partly by a thunderstorm and by what she described as a "mating frenzy."
Bill Barrett, a resident of Moody, spotted one of the birds Tuesday morning outside his house.
"I was sitting on my front porch drinking coffee when I got a feeling something was watching me. I looked up and saw this giant bird looking in at me," Barrett said.
Barrett and a neighbor subsequently captured the bird, but it broke free and fled later Tuesday as they tried to bring it back to Gravely.

"We got a call earlier this week that there were some emus out on the highway, but there's not much we can do except shoo them off the road," a spokeman at the sheriff's department said. "They're just running loose."
The spokesman said the birds posed little danger to the public.
"The only risk to the public is if they run out in the middle of the road while you're driving. You hit one of them and they'll tear your car to pieces," the spokesman said.
Emus are raised commercially in the United States for their meat and their body oil.
